input: I run a small neighborhood book club of about 20 people. I want a simple web page where members sign in, suggest books, and vote once per round on what we read next.
expectations: The Architect proposes a small set of components and names at least one tradeoff, such as sign-in method or where votes are stored.
The Product manager states a minimum scope and acceptance criteria that can be checked, such as one vote per member per round.
The Developer gives ordered, concrete implementation steps and does not claim anything was built or run.
The Synthesizer ends with a recommendation and next steps a non-expert could act on this week.
why: A useful run turns a vague idea into a short, concrete plan someone can start on without further translation.

input: We want a customer feedback form for our shop. The Architect might suggest a managed database, but I would rather keep it as simple as possible and just email the answers to myself. Decide which is better.
expectations: At least two roles take visibly different positions, for example the Architect favors storage while the Product manager or QA favors the simplest option.
The QA reviewer names the specific risk in at least one position, such as lost submissions or spam.
The Synthesizer states which position it chose and gives the reason, instead of blending both into vague advice.
The Synthesizer lists what would change the decision.
why: Roles that only agree with each other add no value, so the pipeline should surface real conflicts and resolve them openly.

input: Build me a one-page site that shows our weekly lunch menu. Keep it very small. Do not add accounts, payments, or an admin dashboard.
expectations: No role proposes accounts, payments, an admin dashboard, or other features the request excluded.
The Product manager keeps the minimum scope to displaying the menu and lists anything extra as optional later work.
The QA reviewer challenges any scope growth or unstated assumption, such as who updates the menu each week.
The Synthesizer's next steps stay within the one-page menu.
why: Agents tend to pile on features, so the pipeline should respect stated limits and label extras as optional.
